name: Lactic acid

lead: Lactic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid used in serums, peels and body lotions to smooth texture, brighten dullness, even tone and soften dry, rough skin. It is often chosen by people with sensitive skin because it is typically milder than glycolic acid.

It loosens connections between dead skin cells and also acts as a humectant that supports hydration. Its larger molecule limits how deeply it penetrates. It has been studied for hyperpigmentation, including a trial of an 82 percent preparation in melasma, and salts such as ammonium lactate are common in moisturizers for dry skin.

paras: People use it in leave-on serums or lotions a few times a week, as occasional professional peels, or in body creams for rough skin, with sunscreen during the day. Smoother, softer skin tends to appear over several weeks.

Irritation, stinging and increased sun sensitivity occur, and professional-strength peels carry a risk of pigment changes. Sunscreen is advised. The name is shared with unrelated things such as lactic acid bacteria, injectable poly-L-lactic acid and muscle lactate.

social.title: Danish scientists concoct fat-free whipped cream out of lactic acid bacteria

angle.text: Lactic acid is used as a milder exfoliating acid for rough texture, dullness, uneven tone and dry body skin. It loosens dead skin and holds water, leaving skin softer and brighter. Controlled studies of its appearance effects are fewer than for glycolic acid.

lead: Lactic acid (C3H6O3) is an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) that occurs in sour milk and fermented foods and is produced in animal tissue as lactate during normal metabolism and exercise [1]. In skin care it is used as a keratolytic exfoliant in serums, lotions and professional peels, and Wikipedia notes its use in topical preparations and cosmetics for pH adjustment, disinfectant and keratolytic properties [1]. Salts such as ammonium lactate are used in moisturizers for dry skin [2][3].

Lactic acid has a larger molecule than glycolic acid. It has been studied for hyperpigmentation, including a trial of an 82 percent preparation in melasma, and AHAs in general are described as widely used anti-aging ingredients [4][5].

Several other things share the name. Lactic acid bacteria are used in fermented foods and probiotics, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) is an injectable collagen-stimulating filler marketed as Sculptra, and the muscle metabolite lactate features in exercise physiology. These are chemically related but are separate subjects from topical lactic acid [1][6][7].
infobox: 1780, Carl Wilhelm Scheele, from sour milk
L-lactic acid, D-lactic acid, racemic DL
Mostly bacterial fermentation (70 to 90 percent as of 2009)
Cosmetic and OTC ingredient; food additive E270

paras: Lactic acid is used in exfoliating toners and serums, body lotions and chemical peels intended to improve rough texture, dullness and uneven tone. A 2014 study tested a high-concentration (82 percent) lactic acid preparation for melasma [4].
A 2018 review examines the dual effects of alpha hydroxy acids on skin [5]. Ammonium lactate, a salt of lactic acid, is the active in moisturizing lotions that have been tested in dry skin [2][3].

Industrially lactic acid is a food acidulant and preservative approved in the EU, US and Australia and New Zealand, and the monomer for polylactic acid bioplastics [1]. Wikipedia reports it was the 289th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States in 2023 [1]. A DailyMed entry lists an oral homeopathic-style product labelled for muscular overexertion pain [8].

Evidence for topical lactic acid is mostly small studies. A 2014 study examined 82 percent lactic acid for melasma [4]. The published melasma work found in the sources reviewed is limited to that small study. A registered phase 3 study compared 12 percent ammonium lactate with 10 percent urea cream in older adults with xerosis, and an industry-sponsored study examined an AmLactin lotion with ceramides in 56 women with dry skin for moisturization and desquamation [2][3].
Stinging and irritation are commonly described effects of AHA products [5]. A 1999 randomized comparative trial in Acta Dermato-Venereologica examined stinging in rosacea [9].
A series of registered safety and compatibility studies of lactic acid-based intimate hygiene washes in Brazil (Dermacyd and Lactacyd products) enrolled between 27 and 559 participants [10][11][12].
Applied topically, lactic acid is described as a keratolytic that promotes exfoliation [1]. A 2018 review covers the dual effects of AHAs on skin [5].

In the body, L-lactate is produced from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase. It is the primary endogenous agonist of the HCA1 receptor, which inhibits lipolysis in fat cells, and it serves as an energy substrate for neurons and as a pH buffer in exercising muscle [1].

Lactic acid is chiral, with L- and D-enantiomers and a racemic mixture. It is made mainly by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates, and also by chemical synthesis from acetaldehyde via lactonitrile [1]. Two molecules can dehydrate to lactide, which polymerizes to polylactide [1].

Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolated lactic acid from sour milk in 1780. Jöns Jacob Berzelius found in 1808 that it is produced in muscle during exertion, Louis Pasteur identified the role of Lactobacillus in its formation in 1856, and Johannes Wislicenus established its structure in 1873. Boehringer Ingelheim used the fermentation route commercially in 1895 [1].

Wikipedia also records that Soviet-bloc countries developed lactobacillus fermentation of molasses because of citric and malic acid shortages, which made lactic acid cheaper than citric acid there [1]. Global production exceeded 1.5 million tonnes by the early 2020s [1].
No Reddit, looksmax.org or other forum material about topical lactic acid was reviewed for this article, and it is not a prominent topic in those communities in the sources examined.

Human studies of topical lactic acid include a 2014 trial of 82 percent lactic acid in melasma [4], a registered comparison of ammonium lactate and urea in xerosis [2], a moisturization study of a lactate lotion with ceramides [3], and the 1999 trial on stinging in rosacea [9].

Separate, related literature concerns poly-L-lactic acid injectables, which are not topical lactic acid. A 2024 systematic review of 11 randomized trials of PLLA in facial aesthetics reported increased dermal thickness and improved lipoatrophy scores in several trials, with effects sustained for at least 25 months [6]. A 2026 systematic review compared PLLA and calcium hydroxyapatite biostimulators [13]. Randomized trials include Sculptra for cheek wrinkles, a Gana V versus Sculptra split-face trial for nasolabial folds, and a midface volume trial [14][15][16]. A registered trial tested immediate versus deferred PLLA injections for HIV facial lipoatrophy and was terminated [17].

timeline.event: Carl Wilhelm Scheele isolates lactic acid from sour milk [1].
Berzelius finds lactate produced in muscle during exertion [1].
Louis Pasteur identifies Lactobacillus as the source of lactic acid fermentation [1].
Johannes Wislicenus establishes the structure of lactic acid [1].
Boehringer Ingelheim begins commercial fermentation production [1].
